title: How the invoke instructions and lambdas reach their targets

questions.stem: A method that overrides describe() calls super.describe(). Which instruction does javac emit, and why does the call reach the superclass version?

options.text: invokevirtual, because the receiver is typed as the superclass at that call.
options.says: invokevirtual would dispatch on the runtime type and reach the override itself; a super call uses invokespecial.

options.text: invokespecial, because it calls the named class's method without virtual dispatch.
options.says: invokespecial is used for constructors and super calls: the target comes from the reference, so the override in the subclass is not chosen.

options.text: invokestatic, because the superclass method is bound at compile time.
options.says: describe() is an instance method with a receiver; invokestatic is for static methods.

questions.stem: How does javac compile a lambda expression such as () -> System.out.println("lambda")?

options.text: As an extra class file like an anonymous class, created with new and invokespecial.
options.says: That is how anonymous inner classes compile; a lambda produces no extra class file at compile time.

options.text: As a static nested class that the class loader defines when the enclosing class loads.
options.says: No nested class exists in the class file; the implementing class is generated at run time when the call site is first linked.

options.text: As a private method plus an invokedynamic call site that LambdaMetafactory links on first use.
options.says: The body is desugared into a method such as lambda$new$0, and the bootstrap method returns a CallSite that is cached for later executions.
